newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major warns of tears if voters reject him.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major warns of tears if voters reject him.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major insisted on Tuesday that a buoyant economy and Britons' fears of a constitutional upheaval could still help his Conservative Party to win a fifth consecutive general election.

In the first of a series of presidential-style news conferences designed to bolster his party's waning hopes of retaining office, Major said a victory for the opposition Labour Party would only end in tears.
"The economic outlook is extremely bright. It would be very foolish indeed were that to be thrown away," he said.
"We have a choice economically between smiles and tears. I hope and believe when the election comes that people will choose the smiles and avoid the tears."

Major's news conference marked the beginning of serious skirmishing between the main parties ahead of the election battle. Labour leader Tony Blair launches his opening salvo at a news conference on Wednesday.
The Conservatives, who have won four elections in a row, are some 20 points behind a revamped Labour Party in opinion polls with a general election due by May 22.

They suffered a miserable start to the new year with one MP denying he had a homosexual fling with a parliamentary researcher and another volunteering to discuss plans for changes to the way Britain is run with opposition parties.

But in a 50-minute news conference, Major insisted that when he calls an election, Britons will look soberly at the programmes of the competing parties, and at the booming economy, and entrust the Conservatives with government again.
He said that despite Labour's pledges not to increase the tax burden, they would be unable to resist increasing public spending if they came to office.
"A Labour government....would probably find it all but impossible to cut public expenditure and it would undoubtedly rise," he said.

Foreshadowing the main themes of the Conservative campaign, he said Labour was likely to give in to European Union pressures for greater powers for Brussels and for social legislation which would hamstring British industry.
While insisting, "Of course, we must stay in the European Union", he pledged to resist changes to the way it worked which were not in Britain's interests.

He refused to bow to Eurosceptics in his party who want a hard line on Europe. "I don't believe when you examine the implications of leaving the European Union that there is any remotely plausible case to be made for leaving."

He said Labour's plans for constitutional reform, including a Scottish parliament and a referendum on electoral reform, could threaten the break-up of Britain and lead to coalition governments without convictions.
"Constitutional change just for the sake of having a so-called radical programme seems to me to be very foolhardy," Major said.
Labour deputy leader John Prescott accused Major of peddling a negative message: "That's because he has no agenda for the future of the country."

Alan Beith, Prescott's opposite number in the minority Liberal Democrats, called for constitutional reforms which would "break the stranglehold of centralised government bequeathed by 18 years of Conservative government".
